title: Integrating Large Language Models and Evaluating Student Outcomes in an Introductory Computer Science Course
extended_summary:
This paper examines how a fully redesigned introductory computer science (CS1) course can integrate large language models (LLMs) while preserving student learning outcomes. The authors argue that coding-capable generative AI tools challenge traditional CS1 goals and assessments, creating a need to reconsider what students should learn and how instructors should evaluate them. The study addresses three questions: how student performance in an LLM-centered course compares with historical pre-GenAI benchmarks, how students perceive learning with GitHub Copilot, and whether outcomes differ across demographic groups.

The intervention was a new CS1 course at a large research-intensive university that explicitly incorporated LLM use, primarily through GitHub Copilot in Visual Studio Code. The course was built around design principles emphasizing use of LLMs, preparation for industry, equity, open-ended projects, and practical computing skills. The curriculum de-emphasized writing code entirely from scratch and emphasized prompting, code reading, debugging, testing, problem decomposition, and large open-ended projects. Quantitative data included exam performance, benchmark questions drawn from a prior international CS1 study, project grades, and regressions by demographic subgroup. Qualitative data came from mid-quarter and end-of-quarter student surveys, including inductive and deductive coding of open-ended responses about working with Copilot.

The population consisted of undergraduate students enrolled in one introductory programming course in the United States. The course ran over a 10-week quarter and included lectures, peer instruction, homework, labs, projects, and proctored exams; some assessments allowed Copilot while most exams did not. Survey participation was partial, with 400 mid-quarter respondents, 315 end-of-quarter respondents, and 207 students included in demographic regression analyses after filtering for complete data.

The main findings were that students in the LLM-integrated course performed similarly to historical CS1 benchmarks on programming fundamentals, with somewhat better performance on an "Explain in Plain English" code explanation item. Students generally viewed Copilot as helpful for productivity, debugging, and learning, especially for novices, but many also reported concerns about overreliance and reduced confidence coding independently. Demographic analyses showed persistent gaps on exams, particularly for BLNPI students and advantages for students with prior experience, but these gaps did not appear on open-ended projects. The authors conclude that integrating LLMs into CS1 can support learning without obvious declines in core outcomes, and that large projects may be especially valuable in this context, though tensions remain around assessment design, equity, and students' dependence on AI tools.

identified_tools.name: GitHub Copilot
identified_tools.description: An AI code assistant integrated into development environments such as Visual Studio Code that generates and explains code from natural-language prompts and code context.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the primary LLM-based programming assistant in a redesigned introductory computer science (CS1) course. Students used Copilot in VS Code for coding, debugging, asking code-related questions, and completing some homework, projects, and one exam component.

findings.finding_summary: Students in the GenAI-centered CS1 course performed similarly to historical international CS1 benchmarks on final-exam programming fundamentals questions drawn from Simon et al. [48]. Across benchmark items there were 535 responses for all questions except Q7 (n=250), and the paper reports one notable advantage: students in CS1-LLM scored 11% higher than the international average on the short-answer 'Explain in Plain English' item (Q7), while other question types were largely similar.
findings.measure: Final-exam performance on Simon et al. [48] benchmark questions assessing code tracing and code explanation
findings.effect_size: 11% higher than benchmark on Q7; otherwise descriptive similarity
findings.sample_size: n=535 overall benchmark responses; n=250 for Q7

findings.finding_summary: On demographic analyses of average summative exam grade, BLNPI students had significantly lower exam scores (β=-8.4021, p<0.001, 95% CI [-12.044, -4.760]) and students with prior programming experience had slightly higher exam scores (β=3.1900, p=0.049, 95% CI [0.014, 6.366]). Other demographic indicators were not statistically significant in the exam model (N=207, adjusted R²=0.216, F=9.107).
findings.measure: Average summative exam grade analyzed via OLS regression by demographic group

findings.finding_summary: For average project grades, demographics did not significantly predict performance in the Copilot-supported open-ended projects. The project regression showed adjusted R²=-0.011 and F=0.670 with N=207, which the authors interpret as suggesting projects may mitigate historical equity gaps, possibly aided by scaffolding and Copilot access.
findings.measure: Average open-ended project grade analyzed via OLS regression by demographic group

findings.finding_summary: Students predominantly reported that Copilot was helpful for completing programming tasks and supporting learning. In qualitative surveys, 69.2% of mid-quarter respondents and 42.2% of end-quarter respondents mentioned that Copilot was helpful (Nmid=272, Nend=133), and 11.5% of mid-quarter plus 8.3% of end-quarter respondents reported it was effective for learning/understanding code or course material (Nmid=45, Nend=26).
findings.measure: Student perceptions from mid-quarter and end-quarter qualitative surveys about task support and learning support
findings.effect_size: 69.2% mid helpful; 42.2% end helpful; 11.5% mid learning support; 8.3% end learning support
findings.sample_size: n=400 mid survey; n=315 end survey

findings.finding_summary: A substantial share of students expressed concern about overreliance on Copilot and possible harm to independent programming ability. In qualitative surveys, 23.9% of mid-quarter and 25.4% of end-quarter respondents reported overreliance concerns (Nmid=94, Nend=80), while 15.0% of mid-quarter and 14.0% of end-quarter respondents said Copilot hindered their learning of programming fundamentals (Nmid=59, Nend=44).
findings.measure: Student perceptions of overreliance and hindered learning from qualitative surveys
findings.effect_size: 23.9% mid and 25.4% end overreliance concerns; 15.0% mid and 14.0% end hindered-learning concerns
findings.sample_size: n=400 mid survey; n=315 end survey

quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical mixed-methods study with historical benchmark comparisons, surveys, and regression analyses, but it is conducted in a single course at one institution without randomized assignment or a contemporaneous control group.
impact_tier_rationale: Impact appears mostly similar to historical baselines, with one descriptive advantage on code explanation and positive perception findings, but no standardized causal effect sizes are reported and some outcomes show persistent gaps or concerns about overreliance.
